questions: What do people say they meet on DMT?

lines.short: Mostly a being, a guide, a spirit or an alien. 69 in 100 said it gave them a message. People who said they'd met God without drugs told similar stories.
lines.but: Only people who'd had such a meeting took part, so we can't tell how often it happens.
how: In 2018, 2,561 adults described their most memorable meeting with a being after smoking or vaping DMT. Looking back, 65 in 100 judged it more real than everyday life.
On DMT, most said the being seemed conscious, intelligent and kind. Still, 41 in 100 felt fear at some point.
It's not just DMT. Of 809 people who said they met God or a higher power without drugs, 86 in 100 called it kind. 78 in 100 said they got a message.
28 in 100 recalled being atheists before the meeting, and 10 in 100 said they were now. Without drugs, the share fell too. But people recalled their old beliefs years later.

has_statements: Only people on DMT describe meeting a kind being that gives them a message.

quick_question.q: After DMT 'being' meetings, fewer called themselves atheists. Did that happen after 'God' meetings without drugs too?
quick_question.why: Yes: the share fell without drugs too, as after DMT (28 to 10 in 100). People recalled 'before' years later.

questions: Can psilocybin bring on a mystical experience, and does it last?

lines.short: It can: most people in one lab study scored as having a full mystical experience. Two months later, 67 in 100 ranked it among their 5 most meaningful experiences.
lines.but: Everyone in that study already took part in religious or spiritual activities, which may have made them see it as more spiritual.
how: At Johns Hopkins, 36 healthy people new to psychedelics took part. 30 got psilocybin once and a stimulant once, 2 months apart, in random order.

Mystical here means high questionnaire scores for things like unity and sacredness: 19 of 30 had a full mystical experience on psilocybin. A trial in people with drinking problems also found high scores.

Two months on, 19 of the 24 who answered said it had raised their wellbeing, against 5 after the stimulant. People close to them saw a small change for the better; personality and mood tests showed no difference.
On psilocybin, 11 of 36 felt strong or extreme fear at some point, and 3 said they'd never want to repeat it.

has_statements: In a lab psilocybin study, fewer than 1 in 20 volunteers felt strong fear.
In a Johns Hopkins psilocybin study, fewer than 5 in 100 volunteers felt strong fear.

quick_question.q: Two months after a psilocybin session, how many volunteers ranked it among their 5 most meaningful experiences?
quick_question.why: 67 in 100 did. All took part in religious or spiritual activities.

questions: What does a meth overdose look like?

lines.short: A meth overdose can look like a body in overdrive. The heart races, breathing speeds up, and people get very restless and upset. Some lose touch with reality.
lines.but: That's second-hand, from two reviews of hospital studies, and how often each sign shows up varies a lot.
how: Signs include a racing heart, high blood pressure, fast breathing and wide pupils. People can be very restless and upset.
The body can get very hot. Chest pain and organ failure can happen, and some people die.
One review found psychosis (losing touch with reality) in 12 to 80 in 100 people seen in hospital. Suicidal thoughts or acts showed up in 6 to 50, depending on the study.
Neither review says how many patients die.

has_statements: Meth poisoning can make the body get very hot.

quick_question.q: Which set of signs fits meth poisoning?
options: A racing heart, fast breathing and wide pupils
quick_question.why: Meth poisoning looks like a body in overdrive, with a racing heart, fast breathing, wide pupils and restlessness.

questions: Does the kind of ayahuasca ceremony matter for how it goes?

lines.short: Maybe a little. People who felt safer and better supported at their last ceremony recalled a bit less fear. They also reported fewer problems later.
lines.but: One survey: people rated the ceremony and how it went at the same time, looking back.
how: Almost 7,000 people who had drunk ayahuasca answered one online survey about their last ceremony.
Each step up on a 1-to-4 rating of feeling safe and supported went with about 0.3 points less fear, out of 10, and slightly fewer problems in the weeks after.
More traditional practices, and drinking in Amazon countries other than Brazil, went with more fear. Church hymns or sermons went with less.
Fasting showed no link the study could detect with fear or later problems. All the differences were small, and nothing was measured before people drank.

has_statements: In a survey of almost 7,000 people who drank ayahuasca, fasting went with less fear or fewer later problems.

quick_question.q: In a survey of almost 7,000 people who drank ayahuasca, what went with less fear?
options: Drinking in Amazon countries outside Brazil
quick_question.why: Church hymns or sermons went with less fear, more traditional practices with more. Differences were small, and people rated everything looking back.

questions: How often do people seek emergency treatment after magic mushrooms?

lines.short: About 2 in 1,000 people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year said they sought emergency treatment, in one big online survey. After LSD: 10 in 1,000.
lines.but: Volunteers answered an online survey about themselves; nobody checked their answers, and people who could not answer were not counted.
how: In the 2017 Global Drug Survey, 9,233 people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year answered this question; 19 said yes.
Of the 19, 13 reported anxiety or panic and 13 paranoia; 8 said they were admitted to hospital.
17 of the 18 who answered felt back to normal within a day, and all within a week.
Those who sought treatment were younger: typically 19, against 23 for the others who answered.

questions: Can other people's cannabis smoke make you fail a urine drug test?

lines.short: Rarely at the US government's workplace limit: after an hour in a smoky sealed room, 1 of 18 people who didn't smoke went over it. At a lower limit, 12 did.
lines.but: One small lab test in a sealed room, mostly in thick smoke; everyday smoke wasn't tested.
how: In a sealed room about 3 by 4 metres, 6 people smoked cannabis freely for an hour. 6 people who didn't smoke sat between them. This was done 3 times, each time with 6 new people sitting in: 18 in all.
Only 1 of 250 urine samples went over the US government's workplace limit. It did so on just 1 of 5 labs' tests.
Some private tests use a lower limit. There, 12 of the 18 tested positive at least once on at least one of 4 tests. A lab check would have confirmed it for 3 to 7, depending on the test.
A positive is a urine result: a THC breakdown product above a set level. It is not a measure of being high.

questions: Do fentanyl test strips show fentanyl when it is there?

lines.short: Almost always, in lab tests: 98 in 100 seized drug samples with fentanyl showed it on the strip.
lines.but: Lab staff did these tests, mostly with one brand. Testing at home was not studied.
how: Two labs tested strips on 106 police-seized drug samples that had fentanyl. The strips showed it in 104.
A lab machine had already found fentanyl in all of these samples. Samples with very little fentanyl were not tested this way.
Strips can find very small amounts of fentanyl. But the smallest amount found differed up to 25 times between studies and batches.
It also depended on how a faint line was read. Trained staff did all of these tests.

quick_question.q: In lab tests of 106 police-seized samples containing fentanyl, how many showed it on a fentanyl strip?
quick_question.why: Strips showed fentanyl in 104 of 106. Lab staff did these tests, mostly with one brand; home testing was not studied.

questions: Can a ketamine drip lift depression within hours, and for how long?

lines.short: It can, within hours. A day after one drip, 64 in 100 were much better, against 28 in 100 after a sedative drip. For most, it faded within weeks.
lines.but: People can often tell they got ketamine, which may make the lift look bigger.
how: In a 2006 trial, 12 of 17 people were much better a day after a ketamine drip. After a salt-water drip, none of 14 were.
In a 2013 trial, 72 people got ketamine or a sedative, picked to make it harder to guess which. Other medicines had failed them.
Pooled trials show the gap is biggest about a day after ketamine. In the 2013 trial, it was not clear by a week.
Two of the 2013 trial's authors were named on patent applications for ketamine in depression. One gave up any share of the money.

questions: Does psilocybin help depression?

lines.short: It may. In one trial, 42 in 100 given psilocybin kept their depression score at least halved from week 1 to week 6, against 11 in 100 given a vitamin pill.
lines.but: People could probably tell they had taken psilocybin, and nobody checked, which may have made the gap look bigger.
how: In 10 countries, 233 adults whose depression had resisted 2 to 4 treatments got a full, medium or tiny psilocybin dose.
After 3 weeks, only the full psilocybin dose showed bigger falls in depression than the tiny dose. By 12 weeks the gap could be chance.
In the US, 104 adults got psilocybin or niacin, a vitamin that makes skin flush. Depression scores fell more with psilocybin, through 6 weeks.
In the bigger trial, serious suicidal thoughts or self-harm happened on every dose, more often on higher ones. The US trial recorded none.

has_statements: In a US trial, one psilocybin session with therapists lowered depression scores more than a vitamin pill did.
In a US trial, people got one psilocybin session or a vitamin pill. Depression scores fell more with psilocybin.

quick_question.q: In a 233-person psilocybin trial for hard-to-treat depression, what did the benefit look like by 12 weeks?
options: A gap that could be chance
quick_question.why: By 12 weeks, the gap between full and tiny psilocybin doses could be chance. People could probably tell what they got.

questions: Did the US government's anti-drug ads stop teens using cannabis?

lines.short: No sign they did. Despite nearly $1 billion from Congress, teens' reported cannabis use stayed flat in a national survey, and those who remembered more ads weren't less likely to start.
lines.but: Nearly every teen saw the ads, so there was no group without them to compare cannabis use with.
how: A national survey interviewed 8,117 US kids aged 9 to 18 at home, and many again up to three times, between 1999 and 2004.
94 in 100 remembered seeing anti-drug ads at least monthly. About 24 in 100 teens said they'd ever used cannabis, in 2000 and again in 2004.
Teens who remembered more ads were no less likely to start cannabis by the next interview. Fewer said they definitely wouldn't.
In one of three periods, more ads even went with more first use of cannabis. The authors call this tentative, not definitive.

has_statements: The US government's anti-drug ads of 1999 to 2004 cut cannabis use among teens.

quick_question.q: Were US teens who remembered more anti-drug ads (1999–2004) less likely to start using cannabis?
quick_question.why: No favourable link was found. In one of three periods, more ads went with more first use; the authors call this tentative.

questions: How many people who use cannabis become dependent on it?

lines.short: About 9 in 100 people who ever tried it, in two older US surveys.
lines.but: The surveys are from 1990 to 2005 and used a narrower definition than today's.
how: A US survey in 1990 to 1992 asked about 8,000 people aged 15 to 54 about drug use and dependence.
Of those who had ever used cannabis, even once, about 9 in 100 had been dependent at some point: fewer than for tobacco, heroin, cocaine or alcohol.
A second US survey, in 2001 to 2005, estimated about 9 in 100 over a lifetime; half of those who became dependent did so within about 5 years of first use.
Newer US figures are higher, about 3 in 10, but they count milder cases and only people who used in the past year.

quick_question.q: In two older US surveys, how many people who had ever tried cannabis became dependent at some point?
quick_question.why: About 9 in 100: in the first survey, fewer than for tobacco, heroin, cocaine or alcohol.

questions: How many people who use stimulants like meth get hooked?

lines.short: It depends how you count. An old US survey found 11 in 100 had ever been dependent; a broader Australian count estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years of starting.
lines.but: Neither survey has a number for meth alone, and the two measured different things, so they can't be compared directly.
how: In the early 1990s, a US survey used set interview questions to find who had ever been dependent on a drug they had used.
Stimulants other than cocaine: about 11 in 100. Tobacco 32, alcohol 15, cocaine 17.
It counted people who had just started, so they had little time to become dependent.
An Australian survey in 2007 counted differently, allowing for when people started. It estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years of starting, but it also counted a related diagnosis called abuse.

quick_question.q: In an old US survey, how many in 100 people who used stimulants like meth were ever dependent?
quick_question.why: About 11 in 100, but the survey counted people who had just started, who had little time to become dependent.

questions: Can drinking lots of water on MDMA lead to low blood salt?

lines.short: Possibly. Low blood salt (sodium) after MDMA has been reported, mostly in young people; of 17 UK cases, at least 10 had drunk a lot of liquid.
lines.but: These only count people who got ill, so they can't show how often it happens, or whether drinking more changes the risk.
how: Over 28 months, 17 people aged 15 to 26 were reported to a UK poisons service. Of the 15 who survived, 10 had seizures, 12 had a normal temperature at hospital, and 13 recovered fully.
The 2 who died, aged 15 and 18, had brain swelling. Both had drunk a lot of water, and drank or were given more after they began to feel ill.
In California poison-centre records, 73 of 188 people who had their blood salt measured had a low level. 4 of those 73 died.
The papers think MDMA makes the body hold on to water, so drinking more than it needs waters down the salt. The UK authors say how it happens is not yet known.

questions: Why do some people overheat on MDMA?

lines.short: Nobody can yet say why some people get hotter than others with MDMA.
lines.but: This is second-hand, from one review of small studies. They couldn't tell heat, dancing and crowds apart.
how: In small lab studies of people at rest, body temperature rose about 0.4 degrees on average at medium doses and 0.7 at higher ones; one person in a group of 8 went up 1.9.
At clubs and parties the average rise ran from 0.2 to 1.6 degrees. But the review reports no comparison of amounts, dancing, room heat or crowds, so which matters is unknown.

Severe overheating (40 degrees and up, sometimes fatal) is known from hospital cases. In one UK report, blood levels didn't suggest high doses. In another case, a friend who took the same MDMA didn't overheat.
People also feel it differently: in one survey, 16 in 100 people who take ecstasy did not feel hot.

questions: Can cannabis cause psychosis, and does using it daily matter?

lines.short: People who use cannabis, most of all daily, get psychosis more often than people who don't.
lines.but: This is a link: these studies cannot show that cannabis was the cause.
how: Seven big studies followed young people for years. Those who had ever used cannabis had about 1.4 times the odds of psychosis later, mostly symptoms rather than a diagnosed illness, compared with people who never had.

For each study's heaviest-use group (from more than 50 times to daily use or dependence), the odds were about twice as high. In two studies of people with a first psychosis, daily use went with about 3 times the odds, and using now and then was not linked.

In a big Swedish study of men, about 6 in 1,000 who had never used cannabis, and about 38 in 1,000 who had used it more than 50 times, later went to hospital with schizophrenia. These counts do not allow for other differences between the men.
Taking other differences between people into account, such as other drug use and other mental health problems, shrank the link by about half.

quick_question.q: In a Swedish study, how many men who used cannabis over 50 times went to hospital with schizophrenia?
quick_question.why: About 38 in 1,000 later did, against about 6 in 1,000 who never used. These counts do not allow for other differences between the men.

questions: Is cannabis stronger than it used to be?

lines.short: Yes, on average. In cannabis from 7 countries, 1970 to 2017, THC, its main active part, rose about 3 points every 10 years in weed and 6 in hash.
lines.but: Most samples were cannabis seized by police, not picked at random, so they may not match what people buy.
how: Researchers combined 12 studies from 7 countries that measured THC in cannabis. Most tested police seizures; two Dutch studies bought samples at random in shops.
A point is a share of the weight: 5% to 6% THC is one point. These numbers describe the cannabis, not what people took in.
Not everywhere: US weed rose in every period studied, but weed in the UK (1975–1989) and New Zealand (1979–1996) showed no clear rise.
CBD, another substance in cannabis, did not change. The authors put the weed rise down to stronger kinds selling more, but sales were not measured.

questions: Does using cannabis as a teenager lower IQ later in life?

lines.short: Not shown either way. In one study, people dependent for years lost about 6 IQ points.
lines.but: Other differences between people could explain it. Twin studies of lighter use found no clear extra loss.
how: In New Zealand, 874 people took IQ tests as children and again at 38.
The 38 people who were dependent on cannabis at 3 or more of 5 check-ups lost about 6 points from their childhood scores. People who never used gained a little.
Another researcher showed that differences in family background could produce a similar pattern. The first team found that family background did not change their result.
In US and British twin studies, mostly of lighter teenage use, the twin who used did not lose clearly more than the twin who did not. These studies could miss a small loss.

has_statements: In twin studies of mostly light teen use, the twin who used cannabis lost clearly more IQ than the other.

quick_question.q: In a New Zealand study, how many IQ points did people dependent on cannabis for years lose?
quick_question.why: About 6 points from their childhood scores, in 38 people. Another researcher showed family background differences could produce a similar pattern.

questions: Do people who use cannabis often do worse on memory and thinking tests?

lines.short: On average they score a little lower than people who use little or none.
lines.but: People were tested only after they had started, so the studies can't show that cannabis caused it.
how: A review pooled 69 studies of young people, about 21 years old on average, who used cannabis often.
They scored a little lower on learning, memory, attention and planning tests. Language, shape and movement tests showed no clear gap.
The gap was smaller in studies that asked people to stop for more than 3 days before the test, and bigger in people getting help for their cannabis use. Small studies found bigger gaps.
In a British twin study, the gap at age 18 was no longer clear when each twin was compared with their own twin.

questions: Do medicines for constipation caused by opioids work?

lines.short: Yes: compared with a dummy pill, more people's constipation got better.
lines.but: Nearly all the trials were in people taking opioids for pain; only one also included people dependent on opioids, so they say little about people using heroin or on methadone or buprenorphine treatment.
how: 27 trials gave people either a medicine or a dummy pill, chosen by chance.
About 52 in 100 got better on a medicine, against 33 in 100 on the dummy pill.
In separate trials against a dummy pill, medicines that block opioids in the gut did better than the prescription laxative lubiprostone; no trial compared them directly.
Diarrhoea and tummy pain were more common on the medicines than on the dummy pill, and slightly more people stopped them because of side effects (about 7 in 100 against 5 in 100).

quick_question.q: In trials for constipation caused by opioids, how many in 100 got better on a medicine?
quick_question.why: About 52 in 100, against 33 on a dummy pill. Nearly all trials were in people taking opioids for pain.

questions: What happened to the famous 2002 study claiming ecstasy damaged monkeys' brains?

lines.short: A 2002 study said ecstasy harmed monkeys' brains. It was withdrawn a year later.
lines.but: Fewer newspapers told readers about the mistake than told the first story.
how: The animals had been given a different drug, from a wrongly labelled bottle.
Two of the ten animals given the drug died during the study.
Of 50 big US newspapers, 26 wrote about the study and 20 about the withdrawal.
The notice does not say what the one animal that got ecstasy showed.

has_statements: When a 2002 study on ecstasy and monkeys' brains was withdrawn, more big US newspapers reported the withdrawal than the study.

quick_question.q: Why was the famous 2002 study on ecstasy and monkeys' brains withdrawn?
options: The monkeys got a different drug by mistake
Other labs could not repeat the result
The monkeys turned out to be fine
quick_question.why: The animals had been given a different drug, from a wrongly labelled bottle. Fewer newspapers reported the withdrawal than the original story.

questions: What about other drugs that raise serotonin?
Which drugs add to MDMA's serotonin risk?

lines.short: One 2007 review ranked drugs by serotonin risk with ecstasy: MAOIs highest, SSRIs lower.
lines.but: This is the authors' judgment from reports and how the drugs work, not from counts of people.
how: Lower risk, the review says: SSRI-type antidepressants and a few painkillers and cough medicines, which it says weaken ecstasy's effects.
Middle: stimulants such as amphetamine and cocaine, and supplements such as tryptophan. Highest: MAOI antidepressants.
Deaths from serotonin syndrome with ecstasy alone are rare, the review says, but harm is more likely with other drugs that act on serotonin.
No study counted how often each mix causes harm. Some people feel little from an amount of ecstasy and take more; no study measured what that does to the risk.

questions: How many deaths does alcohol cause worldwide?

lines.short: Global models estimated alcohol caused about 2.3 to 2.8 million deaths a year, compared with no one drinking.
lines.but: These are computer estimates built on studies of groups of people, not counted deaths.
how: The Global Burden of Disease study estimated 2.8 million deaths in 2016: about 7 in 100 deaths of men and 2 in 100 of women.
At ages 15 to 49, alcohol was the top risk factor in that study: about 12 in 100 deaths of men and 4 in 100 of women.
An older model using WHO data estimated about 2.5 million deaths caused in 2004, mostly from injuries, heart disease, cancer and cirrhosis, minus about 0.2 million it counted as prevented.
A later round of the global study, quoted second-hand, put it at about 1.8 million in 2020. The numbers move with the method, so they do not show a trend.

quick_question.q: About how many deaths a year did global models estimate alcohol caused worldwide?
quick_question.why: Global models estimated about 2.3 to 2.8 million deaths a year, against a world where no one drank. Computer estimates, not counted deaths.

questions: Can drugs be ranked by how much harm they do?

lines.short: Experts have tried: a UK panel ranked alcohol most harmful overall, mostly for harm to other people. For the person using, crack, heroin and meth scored worst.
lines.but: The scores are one panel's views, not measures, and alcohol's top score partly reflects how many people drink.
how: In 2010, experts scored 20 drugs on 16 harms in one day. A 2007 expert ranking put legal alcohol and tobacco above LSD and ecstasy.
Alcohol scored 72 of 100, 46 of them for harm to others. Critics say one score mixes harm per person with how many people use.
Tobacco scored zero for deaths like overdose. Lung cancer was counted elsewhere. The authors agreed it probably kills more than the other 19 drugs combined.
In an online survey, 1,501 people rated drug harms much like experts did. Of the 603 allowed to rate heroin, 467 had never used it.

has_statements: UK experts judged legal alcohol and tobacco less harmful than LSD and ecstasy.
In a UK expert ranking, alcohol came top mostly because of the harm it does to other people.
In a UK expert ranking, alcohol scored worse than heroin or crack for the person using it.

quick_question.q: A UK expert ranking scored each drug for deaths like overdose. What did tobacco get?
quick_question.why: Zero: that score covered deaths like overdose. Lung cancer was counted elsewhere; the authors agreed tobacco probably kills more than the other 19 combined.

questions: Is the change bigger in people who have used more?

lines.short: People who had taken more ecstasy showed less of the serotonin marker.
lines.but: The amounts come from memory, and people who take more ecstasy take more of everything else.
how: Four studies found this link; two smaller ones did not.
In one, each doubling of pills went with a small further drop.
In another, years of use and the biggest dose went with the lowest levels.
Nobody measured how much people really took, or what was in the pills.

questions: Does believing you've had alcohol change how you act?

lines.short: In lab tests, partly: believing they drank alcohol made men drink more.
lines.but: Lab tests from the 1970s and 1980s; the drinking test lasted 15 minutes, with low blood alcohol.
how: 64 men were told at random that their drink had vodka or not, and were given vodka or not, also at random. Half had a history of drinking problems.
Men told it had vodka drank about twice as much in 15 minutes, whatever was really in the glass. Real vodka made no clear difference to how much they drank.
Across 36 similar experiments, believing you had drunk alcohol went with more drinking, but not with changes in mood or memory. Sexual arousal rose on average, but that varied a lot between studies.
The alcohol itself, not the belief, affected memory, coordination, body sensations and mood. Blood alcohol in the drinking study stayed low, so heavier drinking may differ.

has_statements: Thinking you've drunk alcohol, when you haven't, is enough to change your mood and memory.

quick_question.q: In a lab test of 64 men, what made them drink more?
options: Having real vodka in their drink
Being told their drink had vodka
Neither: they all drank the same
quick_question.why: Men told it had vodka drank about twice as much in 15 minutes, whatever was in the glass. Lab tests from the 1970s and 1980s.

questions: Do meth's effects fade while it is still in the blood?

lines.short: The good feelings fade within one dose and within three days; hunger stays gone.
lines.but: All of this used small oral doses in six to nine people in a laboratory.
how: Within one dose, the effects peak in about a quarter of an hour, then fade.
Over three days of twice-daily doses, the good feelings were gone by day three.
Eating stayed down over the three days, while dizziness, sickness and a pounding heart grew.
The body did not clear the drug faster; that was measured and had not changed.

questions: Does buprenorphine help people get through opioid withdrawal better than clonidine?

lines.short: Yes: more people finished withdrawal treatment with buprenorphine than with clonidine or lofexidine.
lines.but: No trial reported people coming off fentanyl, and two stopped early, which may have skewed the results.
how: Fourteen trials put people coming off opioids, mostly heroin, on buprenorphine or on clonidine or lofexidine, by chance.
About 72 in 100 finished treatment on buprenorphine, against about 45 in 100 on the other medicines.
On buprenorphine, withdrawal was milder on average and people stayed in treatment longer than on the other medicines.
There was no clear difference in how many had side effects, but they differed: headache with buprenorphine, dizziness and dry mouth with clonidine.

quick_question.q: In trials, which helped more people finish opioid withdrawal treatment?
quick_question.why: About 72 in 100 finished on buprenorphine, against about 45 on clonidine or lofexidine. No trial reported people coming off fentanyl.

questions: What about other antidepressants?

lines.short: Other antidepressants did not act alike: some muted MDMA's effects, and bupropion did not.
lines.but: These numbers are second-hand, from a 2022 review of single trials with 16 healthy people each.
how: Duloxetine and reboxetine lowered MDMA's rated effects. The MDMA peak in the blood was about 15 to 18 percent higher.
Bupropion did not lower the ratings. The MDMA level was higher too (about 14 percent at the peak, 33 percent over the day), while heart rate rose less.

Some people feel little from an amount and take more. A slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, bodies that differ or a muting medicine can each be the reason. No trial tested what happened then.
The review's authors guess, without data, that bupropion with MDMA might raise the chance of seizures.

questions: What do case reports say about mixing with medicines?

lines.short: In safety reports, ecstasy cases that also named an antidepressant ended in death more often.
lines.but: Voluntary reports cannot show cause, and nobody knows how many people took each mix.
how: In 946 US reports about ecstasy, those that also named an antidepressant had about 1.6 times the odds of a fatal outcome.
Reports naming other kinds of medicine had higher odds still: about 8 times for muscle relaxants and about 7 times for anesthetics.
In a survey of 216 adults, 76 in 100 who mixed ecstasy with an antidepressant still felt euphoria. They also reported more sweating, headache, dizziness and muscle stiffness.
The review's authors suggest, without data, that people whose effects were muted may have taken more.

questions: Do genes and the home you grow up in shape drug problems?

lines.short: Both are linked: what comes from birth parents, and the home a child grows up in.
lines.but: One Swedish study. What birth parents pass on includes the pregnancy, not just genes.
how: In Sweden, 18,115 adopted children born 1950 to 1993 were followed in health, prescription and court records until 2009.
Some birth parents had a drug problem on record. Their children, raised by adoptive parents, had one about twice as often: about 9 in 100, against 4 in 100 when neither birth parent did.
Adoptive brothers and sisters are not related by birth. Still, 6 in 100 of them had a drug problem when the adopted child had one, against 3 in 100 when the child did not.

The study did not work out a share due to genes. Where studies give one, it is about differences between people in one place and time. It does not say how much of your own risk comes from genes, and it can change when living conditions change.

has_statements: In a Swedish study, adoptive brothers and sisters, not related by birth, more often had drug problems when the adopted child did.

quick_question.q: In a Swedish study, how many adopted children whose birth parent had a recorded drug problem had one?
quick_question.why: About 9 in 100, about twice the 4 in 100 when neither birth parent did. Birth parents pass on the pregnancy, not just genes.

questions: GHB or GBL with alcohol: what changes?

lines.short: People who took GHB with alcohol were less awake more often at hospital.
lines.but: Alcohol use was reported, not measured, and the amounts were not known.
how: In 609 emergency patients who took GHB or GBL, 59 in 100 of those who also had alcohol were less awake, against 49 in 100 of those who did not. People who took other drugs were left out. Less awake means a Glasgow Coma Score under 13.
Of those kept in hospital, 55 in 100 with alcohol went to critical care, against 22 in 100 without. Across all patients, that is about 20 and 8 in 100.

Slow breathing (8 in 100 with alcohol, 12 without), breathing tubes (6 in 100 with alcohol, 4 without) and discharge did not clearly differ, but the study could not rule out a difference. Two people died, both with alcohol.
In 16 healthy volunteers, blood oxygen fell 2.1 points with both drugs, more than with either alone. That is a different measure from the patient study.

quick_question.q: Of people kept in hospital after taking GHB with alcohol, how many in 100 went to critical care?
quick_question.why: 55 in 100 went to critical care, against 22 in 100 of those without alcohol. Alcohol use was reported, not measured.

questions: Is 'excited delirium' a real cause of death?

lines.short: The label alone does not establish what caused a death.
lines.but: The cases were selected for reports. They cannot give the risk per encounter.
how: The reviews describe extreme agitation, but no validated definition or specific autopsy sign. The label is also used with living people.
In 168 published cases, force was recorded in 94 of 104 deaths. That included sedation and electrical weapons as well as physical restraint.
Only 3 cases explicitly had no force; 28 had missing information. A later review also cites deaths attributed to the label without overt restraint.
Researchers disagree about restraint, drugs and the agitated state. These reports cannot tell how much each caused.

quick_question.q: In 168 published 'excited delirium' cases, how many of the 104 deaths had force such as restraint recorded?
quick_question.why: Force included sedation, electrical weapons and restraint. Selected reports can't tell how much restraint, drugs or agitation caused.

questions: Do colour tests like Marquis show whether a pill has MDMA in it?

lines.short: In a lab, experts got MDMA right. Two first-time testers made many mistakes.
lines.but: One small lab study from 2003, with a kit and pills of that time.
how: Three lab experts read all 35 samples with MDMA as positive, and nearly all of the 4 without MDMA as negative.
Seven MDMA samples also had another drug, like caffeine or amphetamine. The colour looked the same.
Two people new to the kit tested 8 known drugs. One missed both MDMA samples. The other called four other drugs MDMA.
A review says MDA and MDEA, drugs close to MDMA, give a similar colour. It adds that, read by eye, the tests do not show how much MDMA a pill holds.

quick_question.q: Two people new to an MDMA colour test kit tested 8 known drugs. How did they do?
quick_question.why: One missed both MDMA samples; the other called four other drugs MDMA. Lab experts got MDMA right. One small 2003 study.

questions: Do memory and thinking differences last after people stop using cannabis?

lines.short: Not clear. Where studies asked people to stop for over 3 days, the gap was small.
lines.but: This compared different studies, not the same people before and after they stopped.
how: A review of 69 studies found a smaller gap in studies that asked people to stop for more than 3 days. The gap might be zero, but one almost as big as the overall gap is not ruled out.
Studies of people who had stopped for about 3 to 8 weeks disagree. Some found lower scores on some tests; others found none.
Few studies followed people for longer. In one, people who had stopped heavy use for a year or more did not score differently on any test from people who had not used.
Two reviews read this evidence in opposite ways. Researchers disagree.

quick_question.q: In one study, how did people who had quit heavy cannabis use for a year or more score?
options: Much lower than people who had not used
Slightly lower than people who had not used
No differently from people who had not used
quick_question.why: They did not score differently on any test from people who had not used. Few studies have followed people this long.

questions: Does microdosing magic mushrooms do anything, or is it placebo?

lines.short: In two trials, people could feel a magic mushroom or LSD microdose on the day. But their mood and thinking were not clearly better than with a dummy capsule.
lines.but: Only a small one-week trial used just magic mushrooms; the bigger one was mostly LSD, and neither lasted months.
how: In Argentina, 34 people took magic mushroom capsules one week and look-alike capsules of an ordinary mushroom another. Mood and creativity did not improve.
A bigger study: 240 people mixed their own microdoses, mostly LSD, with empty capsules. After 4 weeks, the dummy group was not clearly worse off.
People guessed right about 7 times in 10. Ratings followed what they believed they took, though feeling an effect may have shaped the belief.
Everyone in both studies took capsules, so neither can show it is all placebo. People might have got better anyway.

has_statements: In a trial with dummy capsules, microdosing magic mushrooms made people more creative.
In trials with dummy capsules, microdosing magic mushrooms or LSD made people's mood better than the dummies did.

quick_question.q: In microdosing trials of magic mushrooms or LSD, how often did people guess right which capsule they had?
quick_question.why: People guessed right about 7 times in 10. Their ratings followed what they believed they took, though feeling an effect may have shaped the belief.

questions: Can touching fentanyl make you overdose?

lines.short: Poison experts call it very unlikely for police and paramedics, and no overdose from touching fentanyl has been confirmed. In 214 news stories about exposed responders, none had proof.
lines.but: Nobody has measured real touches, and finding no proven case is not proof it never happens.
how: Poison experts did sums from fentanyl skin patches, made to deliver it. Powder on skin, they argue, is taken up more slowly and can be washed off.
Researchers checked 214 news stories about police or paramedics exposed to opioids. Only one incident mentioned any test, probably one that misses fentanyl.
A federal safety agency looked into three cases where seven officers felt ill. It found no signs of a serious overdose. No officer had a test that finds fentanyl.
Splashes into the eyes or mouth are treated as a real risk. No sums were done for carfentanil, far stronger than morphine in animals.

has_statements: Poison experts say fentanyl splashed into the eyes or mouth is no real risk.
Poison experts said a quick, accidental touch of fentanyl can easily make a police officer overdose.

quick_question.q: A federal safety agency looked into three cases where officers felt ill near drugs. What did it find?
options: No signs of a serious overdose
Clear signs of a serious overdose
quick_question.why: No signs of a serious overdose. But no officer had a test that finds fentanyl, so these cases can't confirm or rule out poisoning.

questions: How much more likely are people with problem cocaine use to die?

lines.short: Each year, 5 to 62 in 1,000 died: 4 to 8 times others their age.
lines.but: All groups injected, smoked crack daily, were in treatment or arrested; none only snorted.
how: Seven groups in six countries were studied between 1985 and 2005. Each year, between about 5 and 62 in 1,000 died.
Four groups were compared with people of the same age and sex: 4 to 8 times as many died.
Among people who injected, AIDS and overdose were the main causes. In a crack treatment group in Brazil, it was gunshot wounds and AIDS.
Many also used heroin or had HIV, and only age and sex were taken into account. So this does not show what cocaine itself does.

has_statements: In four groups who used cocaine, 4 to 8 times as many died as others of the same age and sex.

quick_question.q: Among people who injected cocaine, what were the main causes of death?
quick_question.why: In a crack treatment group in Brazil, it was gunshot wounds and AIDS.

questions: How do you feel the morning after one dose of meth?

lines.short: Next morning, the biggest dose left people less alert and friendly than a dummy dose.
lines.but: Memory tests showed no change, but the study was small and printed no test results.
how: Eleven people took a dummy dose and real doses on different days in a hospital unit.
Next morning they rated their mood and did memory and attention tests.
After the biggest dose, their heart beat faster and blood pressure was higher than after the dummy dose.
They did not feel sadder or more worried, or want meth more.

has_statements: In a small study, the biggest meth dose left heart rate and blood pressure higher the next morning than a dummy dose.

quick_question.q: The morning after the biggest lab dose of meth, how did people feel versus a dummy dose?
quick_question.why: Less alert and friendly, but not sadder or more worried, and no more eager for meth; one small study of eleven people.

questions: How common is alcohol use disorder?

lines.short: In a US survey, 14 in 100 adults had it in the past year.
lines.but: Another US survey found a little over half as many, so the number depends on the survey.
how: Alcohol use disorder is found with a list of 11 signs of problem drinking: 2 or more in a year count. In 2012 and 2013, a US survey asked 36,309 adults set questions to find it.
About 14 in 100 adults had it in the past year, and 29 in 100 at some time in their lives. About half of the past-year cases were mild. It was most common at ages 18 to 29: about 27 in 100.
The survey's authors think it became more common after 2001. We think their two surveys were run too differently to show that.
The survey missed people who were homeless or in prison, and most people in treatment. For the world, a review passes on an estimate of about 5 in 100 people aged 15 or older.

has_statements: In one US survey, alcohol use disorder was most common in people over 65.

quick_question.q: In one US survey, how many in 100 adults had alcohol use disorder in the past year?
quick_question.why: A survey of 36,309 US adults found this, though another US survey found a little over half as many.

questions: Do people who drink a little live longer than people who don't drink?

lines.short: Many studies found slightly fewer deaths. Compared with people who never drank, there was no clear difference.
lines.but: Few studies made that comparison. So a small gain or a small loss is still possible.
how: Researchers put together dozens of studies. These followed millions of people for years and counted who died.
In most studies, the non-drinkers included people who had stopped drinking, some perhaps because they were ill. People who had stopped died more often.
Six studies started with younger people and compared them with people who had never drunk. There, people who drank a little died about as often.
Allowing for how the studies differed also shrank the gap. Researchers still disagree, and studies like these cannot show whether alcohol itself helps or harms.

has_statements: In many alcohol studies, the non-drinkers included people who had stopped drinking, some perhaps because they were ill.

quick_question.q: Compared with people who never drank, did people who drink a little alcohol live longer?
quick_question.why: No clear difference against people who never drank. Few studies made that comparison, so a small gain or loss is still possible.

questions: Does drinking raise the risk of stroke?

lines.short: In gene studies, more drinking went with more strokes, especially bleeding in the brain.
lines.but: For small amounts it is less clear: older studies found slightly fewer strokes, but the Chinese gene study did not.
how: In a study of more than 160,000 Chinese adults, men whose genes made them drink more had more strokes. The risk rose steadily with the amount.
For each extra 100 grams of alcohol a week (about 14 grams a day), bleeding strokes were almost a fifth more common, and strokes from blocked vessels about a tenth more common.
Women in China, who mostly don't drink, showed no link with the same genes. Most gene studies of people of European descent found the same direction.
Older studies comparing people who drink with people who don't found more strokes at high amounts, but no difference overall.

quick_question.q: In gene studies, drinking more alcohol went with more strokes. Which kind rose most?
quick_question.why: Both kinds rose with drinking in men, bleeding strokes more steeply, in a gene study of over 160,000 Chinese adults.

questions: Do benzodiazepines cause dementia?

lines.short: Not known. In Quebec health records, long use of benzodiazepines was linked to Alzheimer's. A Seattle study that tested people found no clear link with the heaviest use.
lines.but: Neither study could rule out that early dementia, which can bring worry and poor sleep, led to the prescriptions.
how: In Quebec records, 50 in 100 older people with Alzheimer's had filled benzodiazepine prescriptions 5 to 10 years before, against 40 in 100 without it.
The link appeared only with longer use. The records often missed why the pills were taken, and held nothing on education, smoking or drinking.
A Seattle study tested 3,434 older people every 2 years. About 3 in 100 a year got dementia, with the heaviest use or none.
A small extra risk showed up with light or moderate use, not the heaviest. The authors say early dementia symptoms may explain it.

has_statements: Studies have shown that benzodiazepines cause dementia.

quick_question.q: Why is it hard to tell whether benzodiazepines cause dementia?
options: Early dementia symptoms can lead to prescriptions
People forget whether they took them
Too few older people take them
quick_question.why: Worry and poor sleep can come before dementia and lead to benzodiazepine prescriptions. Quebec's study used prescription records, not memory.

questions: Does caffeine during the day affect my sleep that night?

lines.short: After caffeine, people slept about 45 minutes less than on nights without caffeine.
lines.but: The people studied were healthy adults with low to moderate usual caffeine intake, so heavy users, teenagers and older adults may differ.
how: 24 studies compared nights after caffeine with nights without it, in the same people.
Caffeine made falling asleep slower, time awake in the night longer, and sleep lighter.
The more caffeine, and the closer to bedtime, the more sleep people lost.
In five studies, people did not report more time awake in the night.

has_statements: Caffeine added time awake in the night, yet in five studies people did not report more time awake.

quick_question.q: In studies, how much less did people sleep on nights after caffeine than on nights without it?
quick_question.why: That was the average across 24 studies comparing nights with and without caffeine in the same healthy adults.

questions: Do cannabis medicines help with sickness from chemotherapy?

lines.short: In three small trials, more people had their sickness fully controlled than with a dummy.
lines.but: Only 102 people were in these three trials, and most trials had weaknesses.
how: Researchers combined three trials. People having chemotherapy got a cannabis medicine or a dummy medicine (placebo).
About 47 in 100 people on the medicine had their sickness fully controlled, against 20 in 100 on the dummy.
Most other trials compared cannabis medicines with other sickness medicines. The review says these leaned towards cannabis too. But it did not combine them.
23 of the 28 trials had serious weaknesses in how they were run or reported.

quick_question.q: In three small trials, how many people having chemotherapy had sickness fully controlled on a cannabis medicine?
quick_question.why: About 47 in 100, against 20 in 100 on a dummy medicine. Only 102 people took part.

questions: Was mephedrone actually found in the deaths blamed on it?

lines.short: In 25 of 128 alleged deaths, tests after death found no mephedrone.
lines.but: A positive test does not prove cause. A negative test may miss earlier use.
how: By October 2011, 128 deaths in the UK and nearby islands had been linked to mephedrone; 13 results were still pending.
Of 62 deaths studied, mephedrone was the only substance found in 8. Other drugs were common.
One person died weeks later in hospital and had none found after death. Their earlier test evidence is not given.
The authors say tests and incomplete reporting may also miss deaths. They cannot give a death rate.

quick_question.q: By 2011, 128 deaths in the UK and nearby islands were linked to mephedrone. In how many did tests find none?
quick_question.why: Tests after death found no mephedrone in 25. A negative test may miss earlier use, and a positive one does not prove cause.

questions: What is levamisole in cocaine, and what harm can it do?

lines.short: An animal worm medicine often found in cocaine, linked to blood and skin harm.
lines.but: This comes from case reports, so how often it causes harm is unknown.
how: Around 2010 it was in about 7 in 10 cocaine samples tested by US drug police, and in 8 or 9 in 10 urine samples that tested positive for cocaine in two US cities.
In some people the white blood cells that fight infection fell very low. Counts came back 5 to 10 days after the exposure stopped, or sooner with a hospital medicine.
Others had painful purple skin patches, sometimes with dying skin, often on the ears, cheeks or nose. Most healed within weeks of stopping cocaine, but some needed skin grafts or amputation.
Cases were linked to levamisole mainly because the person used cocaine. Since most cocaine held it, finding it shows a person was exposed, not that it caused the harm.

has_statements: Around 2010, most cocaine tested by US drug police contained an animal worm medicine.

quick_question.q: What is levamisole, often found in cocaine around 2010?
options: A numbing medicine used by dentists
A sugar used to bulk up the powder
quick_question.why: Case reports link it to blood and skin harm; how often it causes harm is unknown.

questions: Did US states that legalised test strips see fewer drug deaths?

lines.short: After the law, drug deaths ran about 3 a year per 100,000 people below other states' trend.
lines.but: It looked at laws, not at people using strips. Other changes at the same time could explain it.
how: Researchers used death records from every US state from 2018 to 2022. They counted 15 states and Washington, DC as making the strips legal in that time.

After the law, there were about 3 fewer drug deaths a year for every 100,000 people, about 7 in 100 fewer than expected. Once age, rural living and income were allowed for, this was about the same for White and Black people, though less certain for Black people.
The study did not check whether more people got or used strips. It counted deaths from any drug, and the drop came in the very first month of each law.

The researchers chose the law dates themselves. They kept Alabama, Minnesota and New Mexico among the states without a law, though laws started there in 2021 and 2022, and moved two other dates later. They showed no results with their source's dates.

quick_question.q: After US states made fentanyl test strips legal, how did drug deaths compare with the expected trend?
quick_question.why: About 7 in 100 fewer than expected. The study looked at laws, not at people using strips; other changes could explain it.

questions: How is a death counted as a drug death?

lines.short: Different lists use different rules, so they do not always count the same deaths.
lines.but: The matching studies cover three places. The newest linked data are from 2012.
how: Some lists count drug poisoning as the main cause. Others count drugs found in tests, with age limits.
One death can be counted under several drugs. Finding a drug does not by itself show that it caused the death.
About 49 out of 100 people were on both lists in Norway. Fewer than half were on both in Sweden.
In New Mexico, about 89 out of 100 were on both lists. This study included other poisons too.

has_statements: If a drug is found in someone's body after death, that shows the drug caused the death.

quick_question.q: Two lists of drug deaths in Norway were compared. About how many out of 100 were on both?
quick_question.why: Only about 49 out of 100 were on both; in Sweden, fewer than half. Different lists use different rules.

questions: Does GHB affect my memory or thinking afterwards?

lines.short: GHB affects memory while it works; in one study, people who had passed out from GHB many times had worse memory than other people who used GHB or other drugs.
lines.but: That one Dutch study cannot show GHB caused the memory problems, and nobody checked if they improve.
how: Lab studies found that GHB affects memory and coordination while it is working.
The review says it is not yet known whether these short-term memory effects fully wear off.
One study found that people who had passed out from GHB many times had worse memory than people who used GHB regularly without passing out, and than people who used other drugs but never GHB.

quick_question.q: In one Dutch study, which people who used GHB had worse memory than others?
options: Those who passed out from it many times
Those who used it regularly without passing out
Memory was the same in every group
quick_question.why: Those who had passed out from GHB many times remembered worse than people using it regularly without passing out. One study: it cannot show cause.

questions: Does esketamine nasal spray work for hard-to-treat depression?

lines.short: In two big trials, esketamine spray (a form of ketamine) did a little better than a dummy spray. Only one trial passed its main test.
lines.but: About 1 in 4 felt detached or unreal on esketamine, so many may have known which spray they got, and nobody asked.
how: In two trials, adults whose depression had not lifted on two antidepressants got esketamine or a dummy spray. All started a new antidepressant.
After 4 weeks, depression scores fell about 3 to 4 points more out of 60 with esketamine. A fast start was not shown.
Among people whose depression had lifted, 45 in 100 switched to a dummy spray relapsed, against 27 in 100 who kept esketamine.
The company behind it paid for every trial. Two critics argue relapses may partly be effects of stopping; the trial could not tell.

has_statements: Esketamine nasal spray passed its main test in both of its big 4-week trials.

quick_question.q: Adults whose depression lifted on esketamine spray were switched to a dummy spray. How many relapsed?
quick_question.why: 45 in 100, against 27 in 100 who kept esketamine. The trial cannot tell relapse from effects of stopping.

questions: Is ketamine as good as electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) for hard-to-treat depression?

lines.short: Two big trials disagree: a US trial found ketamine drips at least as good as ECT. But in Swedish hospital patients, 63 in 100 got well on ECT, against 46.
lines.but: Everyone knew whether they got ketamine or ECT, and the trials took different people, so nobody knows why they disagree.
how: In a US trial of 403 adults, mostly outpatients without psychosis, 55 in 100 on ketamine drips said their depression halved, against 41 on ECT.
In a Swedish trial of 186 hospital patients, some with psychosis, 63 in 100 got well after ECT, against 46 after ketamine.
A review combining hospital trials also found ECT eased depression more than ketamine, but about half its data came from that Swedish trial.
In Sweden, 19 of 90 had memory loss lasting over a day after ECT, against none of 91 after ketamine drips.

has_statements: In a big US trial, ketamine drips eased depression at least as much as ECT.
Two big trials comparing ketamine drips with ECT for depression came to the same answer.

quick_question.q: In a Swedish trial, after which treatment did people have memory loss lasting over a day?
quick_question.why: After ECT: 19 of 90 had it, against none of 91 after ketamine drips.

questions: Are lower memory scores due to ecstasy, or to other drugs?

lines.short: In people who used ecstasy but hardly any other drug, memory scores were no different.
lines.but: It was one study, and medium-sized differences could not be ruled out.
how: 52 people who used ecstasy were compared with 59 people from the same all-night dance scene.
Breath, urine and hair tests checked that they had used little else.
Memory scores did not differ, and most of the 40 measures were similar.
People who had used it more than 50 times did worse on one planning test.

quick_question.q: Compared with others at all-night dances, how did people using ecstasy but little else score on memory tests?
quick_question.why: Scores did not differ, in one study where breath, urine and hair tests checked little else was used. Medium-sized differences could not be ruled out.

questions: Do bupropion or modafinil help people stop using meth?

lines.short: Bupropion and modafinil did not help more people stop than a dummy pill.
lines.but: The trials were small, so a modest benefit or harm cannot be ruled out.
how: Putting five trials together: about 1 in 5 had stopped by the end, on medicine or on a dummy pill.
The trials were small and uneven, so a modest benefit or harm can't be ruled out.
A later review of bupropion found about a tenth fewer positive urine tests. This result is uncertain.

quick_question.q: In trials, how many people stopped meth on bupropion or modafinil, versus a dummy pill?
options: Twice as many on the medicines
quick_question.why: About 1 in 5 had stopped by the end, on medicine or a dummy pill; small trials can't rule out a modest benefit or harm.

questions: Does meth damage dopamine nerve cells?

lines.short: Nobody has shown either way whether meth, as people use it, damages dopamine nerve cells.
lines.but: Scans show changes, but those can happen without nerve cells dying. Experts disagree.
how: People who used meth heavily have less of one dopamine protein, but it can drop without nerve cells dying.
Other markers of dopamine nerve endings are not always lower.
In two small studies the protein rose again after people stopped. Other studies found no link with time off meth.
On the other side, two health-record studies found Parkinson's more often in people with meth or amphetamine diagnoses (in one, about 3 vs 1 in 1,000 over 7 years). Some may be other conditions.

quick_question.q: Has it been shown that meth, as people use it, damages dopamine nerve cells?
options: No, it has been ruled out
quick_question.why: Not shown either way: scans show less of one dopamine protein, but that can happen without nerve cells dying. Experts disagree.

questions: Is meth linked to Parkinson's disease?

lines.short: Parkinson's was diagnosed more often in people with a meth or amphetamine diagnosis and no other drug or alcohol diagnosis.
lines.but: It stays rare: about 3 in 1,000 over about 7 years. Some diagnoses are probably other conditions, and medicine side effects were not ruled out.
how: In Utah health records, Parkinson's was diagnosed about 3 times as often in people with meth or amphetamine diagnoses and no other drug or alcohol diagnoses.
That is about 3 in 1,000 against 1 in 1,000, over about 7 years.
A California study found a smaller increase.
The records probably include other movement conditions.

quick_question.q: Among Utah patients with meth or amphetamine but no other drug or alcohol diagnoses, how common was Parkinson's?
options: Diagnosed no more often than in others
quick_question.why: About 3 in 1,000 against 1 in 1,000 over about 7 years; some diagnoses are probably other movement conditions.

questions: Have meth use and meth deaths risen in the US?

lines.short: In the US, meth use rose from 2015 to 2019, and deaths involving meth kept rising through 2023, the latest year counted.
lines.but: Many of these deaths also involved fentanyl or other opioids. The rise slowed after 2021.
how: In US surveys, past-year meth use rose by about a fifth from 2015 to 2019.
Deaths involving meth rose from about 550 in 1999 to about 35,000 in 2023. The rise slowed after 2021.
Medical examiners' reports from 2021 to mid-2024: about 7 in 10 overdose deaths involving meth also involved opioids. This is a different kind of record from the death counts.
The surveys miss people who are homeless or living in places like prisons and hospitals.

quick_question.q: In US death reports, about how many in 10 overdose deaths involving meth also involved opioids?
quick_question.why: Death reports from 2021 to mid-2024 found opioids in about 7 in 10 of these deaths.

questions: Cannabis alone: are drivers who test positive more often in crashes?

lines.short: Drivers with cannabis in a test were linked to more crashes.
lines.but: These studies compare crashed drivers with others, so they cannot show one driver's chance of crashing.
how: Across 28 results from 21 studies in 13 countries, drivers with cannabis found in a test had about 1.2 to 1.4 times the odds of a crash, or of being at fault in one.
An older review found 1.9 times. Re-checking its counts and allowing for other factors brought the same studies to between 1.2 and 1.4.
Studies that allowed for alcohol found 1.1 to 1.2 times. Studies that did not found 1.7 to 1.8 times.
A positive test shows cannabis was in the body, not that a driver was impaired.

has_statements: A positive cannabis test shows that a driver was impaired.

quick_question.q: What happens to the link between cannabis and car crashes when studies take drinking into account?
quick_question.why: Studies that allowed for alcohol found 1.1 to 1.2 times the odds of a crash; studies that did not found 1.7 to 1.8.

questions: Is nitrous oxide (laughing gas) linked to nerve damage?

lines.short: Yes: doctors have described nerve damage after nitrous oxide (laughing gas). In an online survey, about 4 in 100 people who used it in the past year reported lasting numbness.
lines.but: No doctor checked these answers and people chose to take part, so it can't show how common lasting numbness is after nitrous oxide.
how: A review pooled doctors' reports on 100 people with health problems after nitrous oxide (laughing gas): 57 had used it for fun, 25 in surgery.
80 had numbness or tingling and 58 had trouble walking. Of 75 who had a spine scan, 51 showed a change in the spinal cord.
58 of 82 tested had low vitamin B12. But the search only found reports mentioning B12, so this is partly built in.
In an online survey, 200 of 4,633 people who used nitrous oxide in the past year reported numbness or tingling lasting days or weeks.

has_statements: In an online survey, about 4 in 100 people who used nitrous oxide (laughing gas) in the past year reported lasting numbness.

quick_question.q: In 100 published cases of health problems after nitrous oxide (laughing gas), what was the commonest symptom?
quick_question.why: 80 of 100 had numbness or tingling and 58 trouble walking.

questions: Do supervised injection sites reduce overdose deaths?

lines.short: Not proven: near Vancouver's site for injecting heroin, cocaine and other drugs, overdose deaths fell about a third after it opened. Elsewhere in the city, about a tenth.
lines.but: Just one site, before and after, and nothing else was ruled out, such as extra police.
how: Coroners recorded 290 overdose deaths from illegal drugs in Vancouver, 2001 to 2005. About half involved opioids, and about 6 in 10 cocaine.
Within 500 metres: 56 deaths in the 2.7 years before it opened in 2003, 33 in the 2.3 after, about 6 fewer a year.
Critics blamed extra police from April 2003. The authors said that crackdown ended within weeks of the opening.
Critics also blamed the study's start in 2001, a year with more heroin around. The two papers they cited show overdoses falling since the late 1990s, but neither measured heroin's strength or price.

has_statements: A study proved that Vancouver's site for injecting heroin and other drugs cut overdose deaths nearby.
Overdoses were already falling years before Vancouver's injection site opened.

quick_question.q: After Vancouver's site for injecting heroin and other drugs opened, how much did overdose deaths nearby fall?
quick_question.why: About a third within 500 metres, against about a tenth elsewhere, in one study where nothing else was ruled out, such as extra police.
